_meta.what_this_is: A structured argument (claim, inference, evidence, defeater, undeveloped claim) for one question about the lunar habitat: can a flammability ranking of materials obtained in normal-gravity ground tests be carried to the lunar-habitat atmosphere and gravity? It shows how the argument is built and where it rests on documents, on team reasoning, or on nothing held. It gives no verdict and sets no criterion.

C0.text: A ranking of materials by flammability obtained in normal-gravity ground tests can be carried over, in the same order, to the lunar-habitat atmosphere and to lunar gravity.

C1.text: The normal-gravity ground test of the held standard yields a quantity by which materials can be put in order, not only a pass or a fail.

C2.text: The held documents fix one atmosphere, an oxygen concentration and a total pressure, for a lunar habitat at which the order would have to hold.

C3.text: An order of oxygen thresholds measured at one total pressure in normal gravity is kept at the total pressure of the lunar habitat.

C3.1.text: The NASA PSI tests that the team counts for the flammability-limit need record the total pressure of each test.

C4.text: An order of oxygen thresholds measured in normal gravity is kept at lunar gravity.

C4.1.text: The NASA PSI data hold flammability-limit tests recorded at lunar gravity.

C5.text: The combined change to high oxygen, low total pressure and lunar gravity leaves the order of materials unchanged.

assumptions.text: The conditions through which the order could change are the oxygen concentration and total pressure of the atmosphere, the gravity level, and the flow that gravity sets.
Temperature, material thickness and sample size are held as in the ground test.
Pressure and gravity can be examined one at a time before their combination is examined.
An order of oxygen thresholds is what the top claim means by a flammability ranking.

I0.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I0.text: The top claim is split by the conditions under which a ranking is obtained. A ranking can be carried over only if the ground test yields an order at all (C1), the target atmosphere is fixed (C2), the order holds across the change of total pressure (C3), the order holds across the change of gravity and of the flow that gravity sets (C4), and the two changes taken together do not alter it (C5). E0a names total pressure, temperature, convective flow and gravity level as the conditions at which an oxygen threshold is determined; E0b states that fire-limit results do not necessarily apply to conditions that do not reproduce the test. Neither item states this split; it is the team's.

assumptions.text: The maximum oxygen concentration and the upward limiting oxygen index put the same materials in the same order.
The pressure at which a threshold was measured is recorded with it, so that thresholds measured at the same pressure can be compared.

I1.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement

I1.text: Test 1 as written gives a pass or a fail at one atmosphere (E1a, E1b). The same standard defines the maximum oxygen concentration at which specimens pass (E1c), and researchers define an upward limiting oxygen index from the same burn-length criterion and a modified Test 1 that measures it (E1d, E1e). Such a threshold can put materials in order. CP2003.prev.margin states this step: augment the go/no-go criteria with a quantitative test method that provides a ranking or an indication of flammability margin.

assumptions.text: The atmosphere named on the challenge page for a Moon base is the one a lunar-habitat ranking would be carried to.
The atmosphere stays within its stated control band during use.

I2.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I2.text: The items name atmospheres for a Moon base, for landers and surface habitats, or for the most severe spacecraft environment (E2a to E2d). E2e states that design requirements need to specify the pressure and oxygen combinations permitted in the habitable volume. If one combination were fixed for the lunar habitat, the target of the carry-over would be defined. The items do not all name the same combination.

assumptions.text: The change of threshold with total pressure has the same direction and a similar size for the materials being ranked.
The lunar-habitat pressure lies inside the pressure range of the held studies, so no extrapolation is needed.
Results on pressure obtained in normal gravity apply in the same way at lunar gravity.

I3.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I3.text: The held ground studies measured oxygen thresholds of the same materials at more than one total pressure in normal gravity (E3a, E3c) and report that the threshold depends on total pressure (E3b, E3f, E3g), primarily on oxygen concentration and to a lesser extent on total pressure (E3d, E3e). If the change with pressure had the same direction and a similar size for every material ranked, the order at one pressure would be kept at another. C3.1 asks whether the NASA PSI tables could check this.

assumptions.text: The tests that the team counts for the flammability-limit need (rules in pipeline/README.md) are the PSI tests that bear on oxygen thresholds.

I3.1.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I3.1.text: The claim is checked by setting the number of tests counted for the need beside the number of those tests whose total pressure is recorded in the experimental tables (E3.1a, E3.1b). Both are team counts of the evidence package for the lunar habitat.

assumptions.text: Thresholds from short drop-tower tests stand for thresholds in lasting lunar gravity.
The extinction criteria used in low gravity and in normal gravity measure the same property.
The flow in the low-gravity tests stands for the flow in a lunar habitat.
The materials in E4a stand for the materials to be ranked.

I4.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I4.text: E4a prints, for the same materials, thresholds in normal gravity and at lunar gravity; the OF2012 items (E4a, E4b) are the only held items with values at lunar gravity (team search of references.json). Comparing the order of the materials in the normal-gravity rows and in the lunar rows of E4a bears directly on the claim. E4c and E4d compare normal gravity with microgravity, not with lunar gravity. E4e and E4f state that normal-gravity tests do not match flammability in reduced gravity. A shift of every threshold by the same amount would keep the order; the claim needs the shift to be similar across materials, not absent.

assumptions.text: The gravity level recorded for each PSI test (from the investigation's constants in sources.json) is correct.

I4.1.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I4.1.text: E4.1c, the challenge page, states that PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data yet. E4.1a is the team's count of PSI tests for the flammability-limit need in the lunar-habitat package, and E4.1b the count of those tests that match the package's oxygen or pressure and are recorded at the package's gravity level. The claim is true only if the challenge page is out of date or the counts show tests at lunar gravity.

assumptions.text: The order of the materials of E5a under reduced pressure and lunar gravity says something about other materials.
Effects that are small one at a time stay small when they act together.

I5.authorship: team reasoning (AI-drafted), not a NASA statement
I5.text: E5a prints lunar-gravity thresholds for materials whose column heading names the same total pressure as the upper bound in E5b; these are the only held values that combine reduced pressure and lunar gravity. Whether their order is the same as at normal gravity at that pressure bears on the claim for those materials only. No held item measures the three conditions acting together on an order of materials (U5.1).

study_asked.text: A white paper appended to the report (Appendix E-2) states that the lander and habitat recommendations require materials ignition and flammability testing and certification to 34% oxygen. The Executive Summary recommends a modified standard NASA flammability test to generate ignition threshold data, and says lander materials need flammability testing at a maximum oxygen concentration outside the existing shuttle/ISS database.
study_asked.title: Recommendations for Exploration Spacecraft Internal Atmospheres: The Final Report of the NASA Exploration Atmospheres Working Group
study_asked.where: 34%: Appendix E-2 (Scheuring et al. white paper), Conclusion - Recommendations, p. 119. Modified flammability test: Executive Summary, p. 2

U5.1.text: The effect of high oxygen, low total pressure and lunar gravity acting together on the order of materials has been measured.
